name: Serotonin syndrome / NMS

matching.reasoningTemplate: Fever with rigidity/clonus and altered mental state after serotonergic or antipsychotic drugs suggests a toxidrome, not infection.

redFlags: Hyperthermia + rigidity - stop agent, cooling, supportive ICU care

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.3517 (Ch.446/447, drug-induced movement disorders), p.3667 (Ch.463, SSRIs), p.3715 (Ch.470, toxidromes), p.3541 (Ch.451, hypothalamic autonomic disorders), p.3773 (Ch.478, heat illness differential), p.1172 (Ch.149, antibacterial drug interactions)
clinicalPearls: Serotonin syndrome and NMS overlap closely (both cause fever, altered mental status, rigidity and autonomic instability), but prominent myoclonus is characteristically a feature of serotonin syndrome and helps separate it from NMS (p.3517).
NMS typically evolves over days to weeks after a neuroleptic/dopamine-antagonist is started or up-titrated, i.e. a comparatively slow, subacute onset (p.3517).
NMS is not only triggered by antipsychotics: it can also be precipitated by abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson's disease patients (p.3517).
Serotonin syndrome arises from agents with serotonin-like activity or that block serotonin reuptake (e.g. tryptophan, MDMA/'ecstasy', meperidine, SSRIs), and is rare but potentially fatal (p.3517).
The serotonin-syndrome picture is attributed to hyperstimulation of brainstem 5-HT1A (and 5-HT2) receptors (p.3667).
The antibiotic linezolid (and to a lesser degree tedizolid) is a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor: combined with serotonergic agents such as SSRIs it can precipitate serotonin syndrome (p.1172).
Combining an MAOI with an SSRI is an absolute contraindication because of serotonin-syndrome risk; serotonergic agonists (tryptophan, fenfluramine, triptans) carry a similar hazard (p.3667).
Both syndromes are toxidromes in the CNS-syndrome / 'stimulated' physiologic category, alongside lithium toxicity, extrapyramidal reactions and strychnine (p.3715).
harrison.pathophysiology: Serotonin syndrome results from excess CNS and peripheral serotonergic activity - promotion of serotonin release, inhibition of its reuptake, or direct stimulation of serotonin receptors (chiefly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2), occurring alone or when serotonergic drugs are combined. NMS, in contrast, is linked to dopamine-antagonist (neuroleptic) exposure or abrupt loss of dopaminergic tone, producing central hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction; central dopamine depletion impairs hypothalamic (preoptic/anterior) thermoregulation. Both are classified among the hypothalamic disorders of autonomic/temperature regulation (Harrison 22e p.3541, p.3517, p.3715).
additionalDifferentials: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs serotonin syndrome (mutual differential; distinguish by onset speed, neuromuscular pattern and offending drug class)
Lithium toxicity (tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, encephalopathy, may include hyperthermia and seizures in severe cases)
nonInfectiousMimics: Heatstroke / exertional and classic heat illness
additionalInvestigations: Core temperature measurement (most reliable prognosticator of poor outcome in stimulant/withdrawal-type toxidromes)
Creatine kinase (markedly elevated in NMS; rhabdomyolysis complicates both)
Lactate / arterial blood gas (lactic acidosis is a recognised complication)
Coagulation studies (monitor for disseminated intravascular coagulation when hyperthermia is sustained)
Toxicology screen and detailed medication review (serotonergic agents, dopamine antagonists, recent dose changes or dopaminergic withdrawal)
Cranial CT and CSF analysis if mental status fails to improve, to exclude structural or infectious CNS causes
redFlags: Hyperthermia - sustained core temperature elevation predicts poor outcome and can progress to irreversible cellular injury
Rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine kinase
Autonomic instability - labile blood pressure, tachycardia, diaphoresis
Coma, seizures or multisystem organ failure
harrison.prognosis: Both syndromes are potentially fatal; serotonin syndrome is described as rare but able to progress to death, and NMS can be lethal (e.g. typical neuroleptics in Lewy body disease can cause NMS and death). The duration of hyperthermia drives morbidity and mortality, and progression to rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, DIC and multisystem organ failure marks severe disease (Harrison 22e p.3517, p.3715, p.3773).
pitfalls: Mistaking one syndrome for the other: rapid-onset hyperreflexia/myoclonus/clonus after a serotonergic drug points to serotonin syndrome, whereas slow (days-to-weeks) lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia after a dopamine-antagonist points to NMS - the offending drug class and onset tempo are the key discriminators (p.3517).
Overlooking non-psychiatric culprits: the antibiotic linezolid is an MAOI and can trigger serotonin syndrome with concurrent SSRIs (p.1172).
Forgetting that NMS can be precipitated by stopping dopaminergic drugs (not only by starting antipsychotics) in Parkinson's disease (p.3517).

Anchoring on infection: the fever-plus-rigidity-plus-altered-mental-status picture closely mimics meningitis/encephalitis and sepsis, and structural/infectious causes should be excluded if mental status does not improve (p.3715, p.3773).
Dantrolene is ineffective for hyperthermia not caused by malignant hyperthermia, so a hyperthermia mechanism must be identified rather than assumed (p.3776).
Some atypical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine used for agitation) can themselves cause or worsen NMS - adding a neuroleptic to an undifferentiated hyperthermic patient can be harmful (p.3776).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames severity by the physiologic toxidrome state (stimulated vs depressed vs discordant) and by the degree of physiologic derangement on serial vital signs; escalating findings - hyperthermia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and multisystem organ failure - mark severe serotonin syndrome, while marked CK elevation with renal failure and labile autonomic signs marks severe NMS. No formal numeric grading scale is given in the source (Harrison 22e p.3715, p.3517).
